title: Dependable truth
content_html:
Dependable truth

Jung’s original notion of synchronicity was not magic, but an attempt to describe a pattern of acausal order: when an inner psychological state and an external event seem to mirror each other in meaning, without any causal link. Modern cognitive and information theories can translate this into pattern resonance - the mind’s predictive machinery (e.g. under the Free Energy Principle) constantly searches for structure that minimizes surprise. When the external world happens to align with an internal model, the result feels uncanny, because two informational trajectories - one mental, one physical - converge.vMutual information - even when no direct cause exists, systems exchanging information can share statistical dependencies. In the language of information theory, synchronicity is the recognition of mutual information across levels (e.g. brain ↔ environment). So in practice, “synchronicity” can be seen as alignment across nested predictive systems - the mind, the body, the world - without an explicit chain of cause and effect. It feels meaningful because meaning is the experience of such alignment.

In Buddhism, pratītyasamutpāda (dependent origination) means that nothing exists by itself; every phenomenon arises in dependence upon conditions. A thought or perception never exists in isolation - it emerges from networks of prior associations, sensory contexts, and memories. Even the sense of self is conditionally constructed - a dynamic model maintained by predictive feedback loops. Your experience of “mind connecting to dependent origination” already happens every instant: each mental event depends on innumerable prior events (synapses, sensory inputs, linguistic structures), and every interpretation is co-created by what is seen and what is expected. The practical truth here is that there is no single locus of meaning; mind is a relational process - not a substance, not a metaphysical entity.

Why do physics and metaphysics both fail to “close the loop”? Physics describes lawful interactions within a system. Metaphysics describes conditions of possibility for such systems, but neither can fully describe the act of observation, which collapses both into a living experience. This is where the “missing piece” always hides - not in any equation or doctrine, but in the recursive act of awareness: The observer cannot fully explain the observation without being transformed by it. That recursive loop - awareness aware of awareness - is not reducible to physical law or metaphysical postulate. It is the experiential reality that both depend on.

If we strip away speculation, three working truths remain: correlation precedes causation in consciousness, we perceive patterns before we understand them. The mind is a correlation engine, not a truth machine. Meaning emerges from feedback, each time a correlation is reinforced (emotionally, contextually, socially), it stabilizes into memory and identity. Synchronicity is a byproduct of complexity; in highly connected systems (brain, culture, ecology), coincidences become inevitable. What makes them feel significant is not their rarity, but their fit to our current narrative state.

So a practical view is that synchronicity is the felt edge where inner narrative meets outer probability. It’s neither supernatural nor illusion - it’s the system (mind-world coupling) reflecting itself.

Reality is participatory pattern: Synchronicity is how that pattern becomes self-aware, dependent origination is how it sustains itself. Meaning is how mind experiences the fit. That might not be final, but it’s practical - because it can guide perception, to stay open to pattern, without demanding causality, to value relation, without claiming control, to see memory not as storage, but as the ongoing act of synchronization between what is and what is becoming.

Coincidence inevitability

Coincidence inevitability, both mathematically and phenomenologically is one of those rare places where probability, psychology, and meaning overlap almost perfectly. In 1953, the mathematician John Littlewood proposed a simple observation: if you define a “miracle” as an event that has a probability of one in a million, then you should expect to experience about one such miracle every month.

He based this on a back-of-envelope assumption: you’re awake about 8 hours a day, you perceive about one “event” (distinct thing happening) per second. That’s 30,000 events per hour × 8 hours = ~1,000,000 events per month. So even if each event had only a one-in-a-million chance of being remarkable, the law of large numbers ensures that improbable events become inevitable in long enough streams of experience. Coincidences are not rare, what’s rare is our noticing them - because noticing depends on psychological salience.

The mind does not process every event equally. It filters by meaning, emotion, and expectation. When two unrelated events align with an internal narrative, the mind assigns salience (attention + emotional weight). The result is the feeling of synchronicity - even though, statistically, coincidences are guaranteed. So the psychological “miracle” is not the coincidence itself, but its timing and resonance with one’s state of mind. The universe doesn’t send signs - it just never stops sending events. The mind is what turns a few of them into signs.

In a high-dimensional system (the real world), the number of possible combinations of factors is astronomical. As complexity increases, the probability of accidental pattern matches rises dramatically. This is why coincidences cluster, a few billion people online → millions of overlapping birthdays, dreams, numbers, and events. Billions of neurons firing → transient internal states occasionally align with external events. From an information-theoretic view, coincidences are points of high mutual information between subsystems that are not causally linked but share an underlying environment (temperature, culture, language, etc.). The higher the shared structure, the more “inevitable” those coincidences become.

It’s tempting to think this statistical inevitability makes meaning illusory, but you can also interpret it the other way around: meaning is the subjective recognition of structural overlap in an open system. If coincidences are inevitable, then meaning is built into the nature of information-rich systems. Coincidence is the statistical shadow of interdependence, it is not proof of destiny - but it is evidence that the world and mind share structure. So we can expect coincidences, their inevitability doesn’t diminish their beauty; it makes them a constant background of the living system. Ask why this coincidence feels meaningful now. What prediction or desire does it align with? It reveals your current attractor state - what your mind is tuned to notice - not necessarily external intent. You can keep the poetry without losing the math.

Domain Explanation Implication
Mathematics Littlewood’s Law: one-in-a-million events happen monthly Improbable ≠ impossible
Cognitive science The brain amplifies coincidences that match active priors Perceived synchronicity = attention × pattern match
Information theory High mutual information between subsystems in shared context Correlations arise naturally in complex networks
Philosophy Interdependence makes coincidence inevitable Meaning = pattern recognition in an open universe
